results.authors: Montalban X, Lebrun-Frenay C, Oh J, et al.
results.key_findings: Five regions for dissemination in space (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, optic nerve). The optic nerve can be shown by MRI, OCT or VEP. The kappa free light chain index is accepted alongside CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands. The central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions are supporting MRI markers.
results.title: Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2024 revisions of the McDonald criteria

results.authors: Wattjes MP, Ciccarelli O, Reich DS, et al.
results.key_findings: Diagnostic MRI should include the brain with 3D FLAIR, T2 and pre- and post-gadolinium T1, and the spinal cord with at least two sagittal sequences, ideally in the same session.
results.title: 2021 MAGNIMS-CMSC-NAIMS consensus recommendations on the use of MRI in patients with multiple sclerosis

output.summary: The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria (Montalban et al., Lancet Neurol 2025) adds the optic nerve as a fifth region, accepts the kFLC index as an alternative to oligoclonal bands, and allows the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions as supporting markers. Lesions in four or five regions establish dissemination in space without a separate test of dissemination in time; with two or three regions, dissemination in time, positive CSF or the central vein sign is needed. In people over 50 or with vascular risk factors, additional supporting evidence is recommended.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose NMOSD from the cord lesion: it spans one segment, is eccentric and AQP4-IgG is negative by cell-based assay
Do not start a DMT before NMOSD and MOGAD are excluded; some MS treatments (natalizumab, fingolimod, interferon-beta) can worsen NMOSD

Do not attribute the current right leg weakness or the earlier left leg numbness to a lumbar disc: the upper motor neuron signs, the INO and the brain and cord lesions place them in the central nervous system
Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS: cord lesions count toward DIS and separate MS from NMOSD
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria, naming the regions that give DIS and, where needed, what gives DIT or positive CSF (here periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal cord, with the left optic nerve a fifth region by OCT or VEP; four or more regions need no separate DIT).

Check urinalysis to exclude urinary infection (urgency with near-incontinence), then offer high-dose methylprednisolone for the disabling relapse (right foot drop, stopped cycling for fear of falling): oral 500 mg daily for 5 days or, as an inpatient, IV 1 g daily for 3-5 days; consider plasma exchange if severe deficits do not respond.
Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (enhancing periventricular, pontine and cord lesions, a disabling brainstem and cord relapse).

Before starting disease-modifying therapy, check full blood count with lymphocyte count, liver function, HBsAg and anti-HBc, hepatitis C and VZV IgG (HIV already non-reactive), and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before treatment starts
Measure the post-void residual volume for the urgency, then treat with an antimuscarinic or intermittent self-catheterisation according to the residual.
Refer to physiotherapy for the right leg weakness and foot drop, with an ankle-foot orthosis if needed.

differential.key_features: AQP4-IgG negative by cell-based assay; the cord lesion spans one segment and is eccentric; the pontine lesion is at the MLF, not the area postrema; four CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands
MOG-IgG negative by live cell-based assay; no ADEM-like, cortical or conus lesions; oligoclonal bands present
Excluded: lesions in five regions (with the optic nerve shown on OCT or VEP) with enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, after an earlier leg episode
No leptomeningeal enhancement on brain or spine MRI, normal calcium and lymphocyte count, no systemic features
B12 392 pg/mL and normal MCV; asymmetric signs with brainstem and periventricular lesions are not explained by B12 deficiency
No disc or bony compression at C5-C6, and it does not explain the INO or the brain lesions
ANA negative; no rash, joint pain or oral ulcers
RPR nonreactive and CSF VDRL nonreactive

key_clinical_evidence: Left internuclear ophthalmoplegia (left eye fails to adduct on rightward gaze, abducting nystagmus of the right eye) localises to the left MLF, matched by the faintly enhancing left dorsal pontine lesion.

Right-sided partial myelopathy (right leg weakness and spasticity, right Babinski sign, right vibration and touch loss, left leg pinprick loss, Lhermitte sign, urgency) matched by an eccentric right C5-C6 lesion of one segment.

DIS: periventricular, juxtacortical (left frontal), infratentorial (left dorsal pons) and spinal cord (C5-C6) give 4 regions on MRI; the left optic nerve is a fifth region if OCT or VEP is done (left temporal disc pallor without a history of optic neuritis, left GCIPL thinning, delayed left P100). With four or more regions no separate DIT or CSF is needed; enhancing and non-enhancing lesions also coexist.
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negative by cell-based assay, a short eccentric cord lesion and four CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (kFLC index 21.3) argue against NMOSD and MOGAD.
The earlier left leg numbness attributed to a disc without imaging is a probable earlier attack; it is not needed for the diagnosis.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Daniel Rowe is a 34-year-old right-handed man admitted to the neurology service with a 12-day history of progressively worsening right leg weakness and a 9-day history of horizontal double vision. He first noticed difficulty initiating the right leg swing while cycling to work, with the right leg feeling heavy and uncoordinated. Over the following days, the weakness progressed such that he began dragging the right foot when fatigued, and he abandoned cycling four days ago due to fear of falling. He also reports a new band of numbness and reduced sensation over the right leg from mid-thigh to the foot, onset approximately 10 days ago, and urinary urgency over the past week with two near-incontinence episodes. Nine days ago, he developed horizontal diplopia, which he initially dismissed as fatigue. He noticed that it occurred specifically when looking to the right and that the images were separated horizontally. He has not had any eye pain, no loss of visual acuity, and no color desaturation. On further questioning he recalls an episode 18 months ago of left leg numbness and tingling from the knee downward that lasted approximately 4 weeks and then resolved completely. He was told by his primary care physician that this was likely a herniated lumbar disc; no MRI or further evaluation was performed. He also notes that on looking back, his right leg symptoms transiently worsen after hot showers. He denies any fever, night sweats, weight loss, headache, nausea, oral ulcers, joint pains, rash, or sick contacts. He has not traveled recently. His paternal uncle was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis at age 41.

No ptosis. CN V: Facial sensation intact to light touch and pin bilaterally. CN VII: Face symmetric. CN VIII: Hearing grossly intact to finger rub.
